prompt: Describe the dialectical method Aristotle uses in De Anima, specifically how he engages predecessor views while developing his own account of the soul.

result.content:
## 1. Aristotle, Rhetoric, Πάθη, and State-of-Mind Aristotle's dialectical method in *De Anima* cannot be properly grasped without first appreciating the rhetorical and phenomenological context within which his inquiry into ψυχή unfolds. The soul, for Aristotle, is not an abstract metaphysical postulate but a mode of being whose affections (πάθη) are always already enmattered λόγοι—definitional formulae inseparable from bodily life. Accordingly, when Aristotle opens the treatise by asking whether the affections of the soul belong to it alone or also to the body, he is already operating within a rhetorical horizon wherein πάθος designates feelings that alter judgment and are attended by pain or pleasure. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), the soul understood as οὐσία designates not a static substance but rather "a distinctive mode of being, namely the being of" a living creature whose two fundamental aspects are κρίνειν, "separating" from something other and orienting itself in a world, and κινεῖν, "moving itself therein, being-involved-therein, going-around-and-knowing-its-way-around-therein" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 37). This characterization historicizes what Heidegger will later thematize in *Being and Time* as Befindlichkeit, state-of-mind, by demonstrating that Aristotle's treatment of the πάθη already discloses the situated, affective character of human existence. Indeed, the rhetorical tradition furnishes the very vocabulary through which Aristotle approaches the soul's self-disclosure; yet Heidegger cautions that certain sophists misidentified rhetoric's function, for "they do not even know that about which politics is concerned; otherwise, they would not have put rhetoric at the same level as politics or placed it higher than politics" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 107). Aristotle's dialectical engagement with predecessors thus begins precisely by distinguishing genuine inquiry into the soul's πάθη from merely rhetorical appropriations of psychological categories. Burke motives can be adapted "as itself to the purpose in view," functioning as a "eulogistic covering" for what are in reality operative desires and dispositions (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 113–115). Hence the dialectical method of *De Anima* I.1–5, which surveys predecessor views, serves not antiquarian interests but the critical task of separating authentic accounts of ψυχή from those that merely cloak presuppositions in persuasive language. 

## 2. Aristotle, Time-Definition, and Temporality The dialectical procedure of *De Anima* presupposes a conception of temporality that Aristotle elaborates in the *Physics* and that Heidegger radicalizes in *Being and Time*. In *De Anima*, Aristotle asks "whether it is everywhere homogeneous or not; and if not homogeneous, whether its various forms are different specifically or generically," noting that "up to the present time those who have discussed and investigated soul seem to have confined themselves to the human soul" (Aristotle 2014, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). This methodological remark is itself temporally indexed: Aristotle situates his inquiry within a doxographic sequence, measuring the progress and limitations of prior accounts against the fuller articulation he intends. (Heidegger 2009, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. [PAGE NEEDED]), "Being and Time can not be clarified in terms of the 'now'" because "the 'now' is a temporal phenomenon which belongs to time as within-time-ness: the 'now' 'in which' something arises, passes away, or is present-at-hand" (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). Aristotle's time-definition thus presupposes the deeper temporality that Heidegger calls ecstatic, for the soul's capacities—nutritive, perceptive, intellective—unfold not in a mere sequence of now-points but in a structured manifold wherein potentiality anticipates actuality. The innovations in Heidegger's theory of time represent "the very fundamental commitment in Heidegger's theory to a temporal manifold, rather than to a linear sequence of past, present, and future 'nows'" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 124–125). Accordingly, the dialectical engagement with predecessors in *De Anima* is itself a temporal exercise: Aristotle retrieves what has been said, holds it present for scrutiny, and projects it toward the τέλος of his own account. 

## 3. Aristotle, Time-Definition, and Within-Time-Ness Aristotle's dialectical method explains within-time-ness precisely because the doxographic survey of *De Anima* I.2–5 treats predecessor opinions as entities encountered within time—as historically arise, endure, and pass away under critical examination. When Aristotle canvasses the difficulties attending the view that the soul is a self-moving number or a harmony of bodily elements, he subjects each position to the test of internal coherence, asking, for instance, "why does the soul when it resides in air or fire not form an animal, while it does so when it resides in mixtures of the elements, and that although it is held to be of higher quality when contained in the former?" (Aristotle 2014, p. [PAGE NEEDED]). The temporal character of this dialectical move is significant: each predecessor view is encountered as present-at-hand within the horizon of the inquiry's own now, yet it is simultaneously disclosed as past insofar as it has already been surpassed by the aporiae it generates. Heidegger's distinction between ecstatic temporality and within-time-ness illuminates this procedure; as he insists, the "now" in which something "arises, passes away, or is present-at-hand" belongs to within-time-ness rather than to authentic temporality (Heidegger, *Being and Time*, pp. 386–387). Furthermore, the rhetorical and practical dimension of this temporal structure is underscored by the observation that "Mind is not at all pure," being "dependent upon imagination, among other faculties, and imagination is, of course, dependent upon bodily sensation; imagination is the Boden of noein" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, pp. 118–119). The impurity of νοῦς thus binds the soul's thinking to the within-time-ness of embodied life, ensuring that Aristotle's dialectical method remains anchored in the concrete temporal horizon of living beings rather than ascending to a timeless contemplation of separated forms. ## 4. Εἶδος in Aristotle and the Contrast with Platonic Forms The culmination of Aristotle's dialectical method in *De Anima* emerges most sharply in his distinctive deployment of εἶδος, which contrasts decisively with the Platonic doctrine of separately existing forms. Whereas Plato posits εἴδη as self-subsistent realities in which particulars participate, Aristotle redefines εἶδος as the first actuality of a natural organized body. As Papachristou reports, in Book II, Chapter 1 of *De Anima*, "Aristotle describes the soul as «ἐντελέχεια ἡ πρώτη σώματος φυσικοῦ ὀργανικοῦ» («the first actuality of a natural organic" body) (Papachristou, *Three Kinds or Grades of Phantasia in Aristotle's De Anima*, pp. 1–3). The soul qua εἶδος is thus inseparable from the matter it informs; it is not a transcendent paradigm but the very organizational principle that makes a body alive. This reconfiguration is achieved dialectically: Aristotle first entertains and then dismantles predecessor views—materialist, dualist, and Platonic alike—exposing the absurdities that follow from treating the soul as either pure matter or pure form subsisting apart. Heidegger captures this methodological trajectory when the ἕξις structure is primary, meaning that the "direction of being-interpretation runs through the categories of ἕξις, being as determinate 'having,' 'having something at one's disposal'" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 160). The soul's εἶδος is thus a having—a first actuality analogous to possessing knowledge before exercising it—rather than a separable substance. Indeed, Caston observes that Aristotle directs "our attention to the widespread phenomenon of error and challenges his predecessors" precisely phantasia, an operation of the soul's εἶδος, cannot be reduced to mere perception or opinion (Caston, *Why Aristotle Needs Imagination*, pp. 3–4). The tension between universal form and individual substance—whether εἶδος is shared across instances or must be particular—remains productively unresolved, yet the dialectical method ensures that Aristotle's account of the soul as enmattered form stands as a genuine philosophical advance over Platonic separation.
